title: Avenue Montaigne (Fauteuils D'Orchestre)
full_review:
For years, films showing off Paris at its most glamorous were a staple of cinema screens.

The French-language "Avenue Montaigne" ("Fauteuils D'Orchestre") (ThinkFilm) is something of a colorful throwback to that genre, with a bit more serious intent beneath the gloss.

A bittersweet comedy-drama, it centers on a gaminelike young woman, Jessica (Cecile de France), who in the opening scenes bids adieu to Madame Roux (Suzanne Flon), the beloved grandmother who raised her, and takes off for Paris.

After several rejections elsewhere, she talks her way into a waitress job in a popular bistro, the Bar des Theatres, on the stylish titular boulevard, and in her guileless way eventually becomes a catalyst for several of the regular customers.

These include Jean-Francois Lefort (Albert Dupontel), a classical pianist facing a midlife crisis in his career and marriage to an overly controlling wife, Valentine (Laura Morante); good-looking Fred (Christopher Thompson, the director's son and the film's co-writer), who learns that his mistress, Valerie (Annelise Hesme), has moved on to his father, Jacques Grumberg (Clause Brasseur), a widower with cancer poignantly auctioning off the art collection he had amassed with his late wife; Catherine (Valerie Lemercier), a popular (and temperamental) soap opera star about to open onstage in a Feydeau revival but longing to gain serious credentials by playing writer Simone de Beauvoir in a new biopic for Hollywood director Brian Sobinski (Sydney Pollock); and a theater concierge, Claudie (Dani), on the eve of her retirement.

Director and co-writer Daniele Thompson conveys a canny empathy with her characters, all searching to fill the emptiness in their lives. The performances project the uncanny ring of truth.

Subtitles.

The film contains sporadic rough and crude language and expressions, an implication of adultery, premarital relationships, sexual banter and the acceptability of divorce. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
